in_text_mentions: SMS involves distinctive facial dysmorphia (Fig. 1). Children with SMS often have light-colored hair, bulging forehead, moderate hypoplasia of the middle part of the face and nasal bridge, hypertelorism, oblique outer and upper palpebral fissures, and synophrys. Micrognathia — readily observed during the first years of life — reverses over time, tending towards prognathism characterized by a wide, square-shaped face (Fig. 1). It may be associated with dental anomalies such as tooth agenesis (especially premolar teeth), and/or taurodontism. The child should be tested for ogival palate, short ve

About two thirds of young patients are of short stature. The limbs are short, with brachydactyly (Fig. 1). Some cases also show limited elbow-extension span, clinodactyly of the fifth finger, syndactyly of the second and third toes, persistence of fetal pads, and polydactyly. Scoliosis is frequent and should be systematically screened via clinical examination and spinal cord X-rays. Android obesity often appears in adolescence [2, 19–21]. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Posteroanterior radiograph of the spine showing thoracic scoliosis (85°) and lumbar scoliosis (80°) in a patient with Smith-Magenis syndrome. The article is a case report specifically on surgical treatment of scoliosis in Smith-Magenis syndrome, and scoliosis is a well-documented manifestation of this condition. B: Lateral radiograph of the spine showing increased thoracic kyphosis in a patient with Smith-Magenis syndrome. The article is a case report specifically on surgical treatment of scoliosis in Smith-Magenis syndrome, and kyphoscoliosis is a well-documented manifestation of this condition.
panels.attribution_text: Tsirikos et al. Surgical treatment of scoliosis in Smith-Magenis syndrome: a case report.. Journal of medical case reports 2010. doi:10.1186/1752-1947-4-26. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Preoperative posteroanterior (A) and lateral (B) radiographs of the spine show a thoracic and lumbar scoliosis measuring 85 and 80° respectively with increased thoracic kyphosis.
in_text_mentions: Our patient underwent a posterior spinal arthrodesis extending from T3 to L4 with a double pedicle hook/screw and rod construct six months following initial clinical assessment and while the scoliosis had further progressed (Figure 1). An interfacetal and intertransverse arthrodesis was performed bilaterally at every level across the instrumentation using iliac crest graft supplemented by allograft bone. Spinal cord monitoring was performed during the surgery recording somatosensory (SSEP) and motor (MEP) evoked potentials and there were no problems.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Standing anteroposterior preoperative spine radiograph of a 13-year-old girl with Smith-Magenis syndrome showing a left upper thoracic scoliosis (T1-T7, Cobb 74°) and right main thoracic curve (T7-L1, Cobb 60°), directly captioned and described in text as the patient's scoliosis; a human-patient radiological image of a recognized SMS manifestation (scoliosis with vertebral anomaly). B: Standing lateral preoperative spine radiograph of the same 13-year-old girl with Smith-Magenis syndrome, part of the captioned anteroposterior and lateral radiograph pair, showing the sagittal profile of her scoliotic spine with annotated Cobb-angle lines; human-patient radiological image of an SMS-associated manifestation.

in_text_mentions: We present the case of a 13-year-old girl who was admitted for the correction of her scoliosis. Her plain radiographs of the spine showed a thoracic scoliosis with a Cobb angle of 74° (Figure 1), suggesting the need for surgical correction.

itial assessment in our clinic revealed a left upper thoracic scoliosis extending from T1 to T7 and measuring 74° and a right main thoracic scoliosis extending from T7 to L1 and measuring 60° (Figure 1). The Risser grade was I, indicating that the patient had a significant amount of remaining growth and this could result in further deterioration of her scoliosis. Eyes are anonymized with black bars, which is de-identification, not a diagnostic annotation. A: Whole-body photograph of the confirmed SMS patient; in-text evidence documents helmet use for frequent falls and a vest for spine deformity. No single vocabulary finding is clearly assessable at this scale, but the panel documents the patient's overall phenotype and supportive equipment. B: Facial photograph while smiling of the SMS patient; the everted/tented upper lip is a classic SMS facial feature, though partially obscured by glasses and protective helmet. C: Frontal facial photograph of the same SMS patient; dysmorphic features are limited by the protective helmet, privacy bar and glasses, but the broad midface and open-mouth posture are consistent with the SMS facies. D: Photograph documenting the patient's behavior; the in-text description states he was 'more entertained by the toys and games on a cellular phone than by the visitors', a recognized SMS behavioral phenotype (object play/self-stimulatory behavior).
